paper_title: BrickWright: Agentic Creation of Physically Feasible Brick Builds

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Frontier coding agents are becoming increasingly adept at 3D modeling. Yet, they still face challenges when building objects meant to be assembled in the physical world, often creating invalid assemblies with floating, colliding, or disconnected parts. We argue that providing agents with tools for assembling builds and verifying their physical feasibility is sufficient for them to produce physically valid assemblies that still adhere to input prompts. Focusing on the domain of LEGO brick builds, we present BrickWright, a framework for generating physically feasible brick builds from text or image prompts using pre-trained agents, where a build is physically feasible if it uses only real parts, has no colliding or floating parts, and forms a connected structure if possible. BrickWright guides agents to create builds by writing code with BrickLayer, a Python toolkit with two main components: an ergonomic brick assembly API that halves inference cost compared to working in raw LDraw, and a validator that provides feedback on physical feasibility. Whereas baseline agents achieve physical validity rates ranging from only 9% (GPT-6 Luna) to 69% (GPT-6 Astra), BrickWright-guided agents achieve 100% validity on a sample of 512 prompts, while improving prompt adherence for lightweight agents and maintaining it for stronger agents. Additionally, they outperform specialized models on the text-to-brick task. Code is available on our project page: https://avalovelace1.github.io/brickwright/

sections.title: Start
sections.content: BrickWright: Agentic Creation of Physically Feasible Brick Builds Ava Pun1 Kevin Dai1 Sally Chen1 Maxwell Jones1 Ruixuan Liu1 Kangle Deng2 Changliu Liu1 Maneesh Agrawala3 Deva Ramanan1 Jun-Yan Zhu1 1Carnegie Mellon University 2Independent Researcher 3Stanford University Figure 1. BrickWright overview. BrickWright instructs pre-trained LLM agents to generate physically feasible brick builds by writing code using Python SDK, BrickLayer, in plan-execute-validate loop utilizing BrickLayers physical validation tools (a). BrickWright accepts text or image inputs and can produce articulated and large-scale builds, all physically valid. Agents equipped with BrickWright produce higher-quality builds with fewer physical violations (b). Red outlines in insets indicate mesh intersections.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Frontier coding agents are becoming increasingly adept at 3D modeling. Yet, they still face challenges when building objects meant to be assembled in the physical world, often creating invalid assemblies with floating, colliding, or disconnected parts. We argue that providing agents with tools for assembling builds and verifying their physical feasibility is sufficient for them to produce physically valid assemblies that still adhere to input prompts. Focusing on the domain of LEGO brick builds, we present BrickWright, framework for generating physically feasible brick builds from text or image prompts using pre-trained agents, where build is physically feasible if it uses only real parts, has no colliding or floating parts, and forms connected structure if possible. BrickWright guides agents to create builds by writing code with BrickLayer, Python toolkit with two main components: an ergonomic brick assembly API that halves inference cost compared to working in raw LDraw, and validator that provides feedback on physical feasibility. Whereas baseline agents achieve physical validity rates ranging from only 9% (GPT-6 Luna) to 69% (GPT-6 Astra), BrickWright-guided agents achieve 100% validity on sample of 512 prompts, while improving prompt adherence for lightweight agents and maintaining it for stronger agents. Additionally, they outperform specialized models on the text-to-brick task. Code is available on our project page: avalovelace1.github.io/brickwright. 1. Introduction Large language model (LLM) agents are becoming increasingly adept at 3D modeling. Without additional fine-tuning, commercially available agents can successfully produce articulated objects [45, 59], scenes [52], and constructive solid geometry models [27]. However, they still face challenges 1 constraints, they generally exhibit worse generalization and lower fidelity than commercial LLM agents on the same task. Hence, we wish to achieve this task agentically. Toward this goal, we introduce BrickLayer, Python package for assembling and validating brick builds, alongside BrickWright, framework that guides LLM agents through creating validated brick builds with BrickLayer. Agents equipped with BrickWright create higher-quality builds with fewer physical violations; on test set of 512 prompts, all agentsincluding lightweight models like GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5achieve 100% validity score without significant cost increase or drop in fidelity. BrickWright is especially useful for lightweight models: it improves Lunas performance from 9% to 100% valid builds and boosts its prompt adherence at 2% the price of frontier models. BrickWright additionally outperforms specialized brick generation models on validity and fidelity. Code is available on our project page: avalovelace1.github.io/brickwright. 2. Related work Brick Build Generation. Early work treats brick build generation as an optimization problem over target shape. Legolization [34] voxelizes 3D mesh, merges voxels into standard bricks, and iteratively re-merges regions identified as unstable. Subsequent work captures finer geometric detail through feature-aware shape approximation and nonrectangular bricks [57, 58], assembles bricks sequentially via Bayesian optimization [17], or optimizes Technic assemblies to match annotated sketches [49]. Retrieval-based methods map images to figurines assembled from prebuilt templates [9, 56]. These methods are limited by small brick vocabularies, explicit geometric guidance, or fixed templates. Learning-based methods generate brick structures directly from data. These approaches adapt graph generative models [41], predict voxel representations that are assembled into bricks algorithmically [4, 24], learn sequential construction policies [7], or use diffusion to predict labeled voxels within single category [10]. Autoregressive methods generate bricks conditioned on text or images. BrickGPT [37] fine-tunes an LLM to generate stable structures, but is restricted to eight rectangular brick types across 21 object categories. LEGO-Maker [11] generates builds from images, but supports only axis-aligned orientations and two categories. LegoACE [50] and BrickNet [19] scale to openvocabulary generation by training on large collections of human-designed builds. However, LegoACE learns connectivity implicitly and can produce disconnected components, while BrickNet represents assemblies as connector graphs but accumulates collisions over longer build sequences. Brick-Composer [30] instead approaches assembly from target views as sequential brick selection and pose estimation, Figure 2. Physical violations in builds by Codex (GPT-6 Astra, high reasoning). Red outlines in insets show mesh intersections. when building objects for the physical world. We focus on the task of creating multi-part assemblies: real-world objects made from set of prefabricated parts joined by fixed connectors, such as LEGO builds. Multi-part assemblies must obey multiple constraints: all parts must be drawn from preset library, parts must not collide or float, and the joined parts typically form single connected component. We argue that designing toolkit for multi-part assembly creation is sufficient to enable agents to create physically valid builds. This toolkit should include (1) an assembly API, which provides an ergonomic programmatic interface for 3D creation; and (2) validator, which provides feedback on finished builds physical validity. The need for toolkit is independent of how powerful coding agent is. We observe that GPT-6 Astra with Codex, when asked to make brick builds, already writes scripts to generate and validate its output more than 80% of the time (Sec. D). For complex physical domains, this self-validation is often not enough, resulting in builds that do not satisfy physical constraints, containing colliding, floating, or disconnected parts  (Fig. 2)  . Even if an agent is powerful enough to write perfect toolkit, separately developing toolkit remains important to reduce token usage and avoid repeated work. Existing toolkits for agentic 3D generation [45, 59] are usually intended for digital asset creation; as they do not consider physical constraints, they cannot be repurposed as-is to create real-world objects. We focus on the domain of LEGO generation as it is commonly available yet complex system, consisting of thousands of parts that connect in dozens of ways. Our key insight is to merge agentic code-as-3D-models with the regularity of brick parts. Parts can be modeled as geometries with localized connectors that have programmatic rules for assembly (e.g., studs interlock with antistuds). From this perspective, we leverage the physical production rules for snap-fit brick builds [6] to create an ergonomic assembly API. Then, given an image or text prompt, our task is to generate program using this API that, when compiled, produces LEGO brick build in the standard LDraw format [21]. This build should include list of library part placements, and it must be physically feasible, having no intersecting or floating parts and forming connected structure if possible. While there are several specialized brick generation methods [10, 11, 19, 36, 37, 48, 50, 53], some of which consider physical 2 Figure 3. Method overview. (a) BrickLayer supports catalog discovery, compositional construction with typed connectors, and physical validation. (b) BrickWright prompts pre-trained LLM agent to write and revise build.py, which contains brick build creation code and agent-defined tests. The validate tool runs fixed collision and floating checks alongside the agents tests, while the render tool provides views for visual inspection. The agent calls finalize once all checks pass. The agent may optionally run explore at any time to investigate the BrickLayer API and written brick build. Arrows summarize information flow rather than fixed tool-call sequence. training multimodal LLM on simulator-generated data and feedback. Other methods improve buildability through preference optimization or reinforcement learning [36, 48]. In contrast, BrickWright utilizes pre-trained models to build arbitrary objects without task-specific training, verifies collisions and connectivity in feedback loop, and supports articulation. Concurrent with our work, BrickBench [20] introduces toolkit for agentic brick build creation, focusing on benchmarking the performance of different agents. Agentic 3D Generation. LLM agents have been used successfully to create 3D scenes. Recent works use planexecute-critique loop [15, 29] or reconstruct scenes from images through iterative code execution and visual inspection [13, 52]. Other works fine-tune LLMs to reason directly over 3D spatial inputs [44] or to generate tool-call trajectories [14]. These methods place objects in continuous space and rely on optimization or visual judgment to resolve collisions and floating objects. In BrickWright, explicit connector rules enable deterministic checks of attachment validity. Representing shapes as programs provides structured descriptions of geometry and part relationships [16, 39, 42]. Separately, LLMs have been shown to reason more reliably when they write code and offload exact computation to an interpreter [8]. Building on both ideas, agents have been applied to modeling individual objects as code, typically through plan-execute-critique loops. Prior work augments this loop with API retrieval [32], domain-specific languages [45], or procedural part-based modeling [27], with some supporting articulation [23, 27, 45, 59]. In CAD, LLMs have been fine-tuned to generate parametric modeling code [12, 18, 47], while tool-augmented agents generate and refine parts and assemblies [1, 35, 40, 55]. Articraft [59] generates articulated assets using custom SDK and minimal harness that provides textual feedback from tools that probe the model code. Unlike these systems, where the agent generates geometry or infers inter-part relationships, BrickWright assembles fixed parts whose connectors determine how they attach and move. Physics-Aware Generation. To improve physical validity, prior work refines shapes or layouts after generation [5, 25, 29, 51, 54], fine-tunes generators on simulator feedback [26], or guides diffusion sampling with physical constraints [33]. Geometric analysis has also been used to plan LEGO assembly sequences without explicit connector information [2]. For brick structures, stability has been assessed through force-based equilibrium analysis [31, 34, 37] or physics simulation [17, 46]. In contrast, BrickWright uses an executable verifier to check for collisions, floating parts, and connectivity, allowing pre-trained agent to iteratively repair builds without task-specific training. Incorporating force-based stability analysis [31, 34] is natural extension. 3. BrickWright Given natural-language or image description, our task is to generate physically feasible brick build from fixed part catalog. brick build is defined as an ordered sequence of placements. Each placement consists of an element or nested brick build, together with rigid transformation relative to the containing build. An element specifies single part drawn from the catalog and color. Elements expose typed connectors, such as studs, whose compatibility and relative alignment determine valid connections. build is 3 valid if it uses only catalog parts and contains no colliding (intersecting) or floating parts. It forms connected component if one can draw path of connections between any two elements in the build. We define build to be physically feasible if it is valid and contains as few connected components as possible. More complex feasibility considerations, such as ensuring build is stable and has an executable assembly sequence, are left to future work. Note that although having single connected component is desirable as it makes build less likely to break apart in the physical world, builds with multiple components are still necessary in some cases: for example, two separate vehicles in car chase scene. We introduce BrickWright  (Fig. 3)  , framework for generating physically feasible brick builds using LLM agents. Using lightweight harness, BrickWright guides single agent to write Python code that produces brick build using custom toolkit called BrickLayer. If the build passes set of predefined and agent-written tests, it is accepted; otherwise, the agent makes edits informed by the test results, following the commonly used plan-execute-validate loop. 3.1. BrickLayer LDraw [21], the standard text format for LEGO builds, includes no physical validation and is not very ergonomic: it only allows users to place parts and sub-models by their absolute 3D poses. This makes it difficult to mate parts by their connectors or place them relative to others, which can lead to wasted tokens and misplaced components. To provide agents with an ergonomic interface for creating and validating brick builds, we introduce BrickLayer (Listing 1), Python package that includes functions for part discovery, assembly, and validation. BrickLayer provides unified programmatic representation for brick builds, enabling them to be easily understood and edited by humans and agents; builds can be translated from BrickLayer to LDraw and vice versa. See Sec. for BrickLayer documentation. Discovery. BrickLayer allows users to search the LDraw catalog [22], which contains 17k+ parts. This search accepts keywords matched against the parts official LDraw name. Results are ordered by their BM25 score [38] multiplied by popularity factor that scales logarithmically with the number of official LEGO sets containing the part. LDraw names are parsed into fields such as category, subcategory, and dimensions; users may target specific fields with their keyword search and filter results using exact field matches. Assembly. The central objects of BrickLayer are Element, representing single colored part, and LegoBuild, representing brick build. Both objects support unified LegoGeometry interface; this interface exposes dimensions and available connectors, which can be filtered by type and position. We use BrickNets connector annotations [19], which mark the local frames of the connectors on each part, = LegoBuild() # Initialize build socket = b.add(Element("14418", Color.ORANGE)) ball = Element("3170", Color.MEDIUM_AZURE) b.connect( # Search for and mate compatible connectors ball, ball.find_connector("towball", toward=Direction.RIGHT), to=socket.find_connector("towball_socket") ) assert (not b.colliding_placements # Check feasibility and not b.floating_placements and len(b.connected_components == 1) write_ldraw(b, "build.ldr") # Export to LDraw Output LDraw: 1 25 20 -8 10 1 0 0 0 1 0 0 0 1 14418.dat 1 322 80 -8 10 1 0 0 0 1 0 0 0 1 3170.dat Listing 1. BrickLayer usage. Users can add elements, join them via selected connectors, and assess feasibility. The BrickLayer script is easier to understand than its corresponding LDraw output. along with compatible connector types and the joints they form: fixed, revolute, ball, prismatic, or cylindrical. For example, studs and antistuds join with revolute joint. As BrickNet annotations do not differentiate between prismatic and cylindrical joints, we determine sliding joints type by rotating it 15 about its axis in one direction; if collision occurs, we mark the joint prismatic. LegoBuilds have recursive structure: they may contain both Elements and other LegoBuilds, allowing complex models to be built from smaller components. Placements can be made at arbitrary poses, fixed to grid, or by mating specified connectors. Users may name placements, allowing them to place components relative to or directly target the connectors of named component. Users may also explicitly mark movable components with articulation limits corresponding to their joint type. For convenience, BrickLayer includes several high-level construction functions, introduced after noting repeated patterns in agent-generated code. These include brick, plate, tile, slope, and inverted slope to instantiate common parts by specifying their dimensions; minifigure, door, and window to create common multi-component sub-builds; mirror to reflect build along given axis; and fill box, fill slope, and fill inverted slope to fill cuboid or wedge in manner guaranteed to be valid and connected if possible. Validation. LegoBuild provides methods to list collisions, floating elements, and disconnected components. To determine whether two elements collide, we inset each mesh by 0.1 mm before checking for intersections, following BrickNet; snap connections between bricks are so tight that naive mesh intersection check would report false positive. The floater check first translates build so its lowest point is at the ground plane. Then, it marks an element floating if it cannot reach grounded element through mated connectors 4 Table 1. Two connectors form connection if their local frames align, depending on their joint type; for example, fixed joint requires the two frames to align exactly, while revolute joint additionally admits rotational degree of freedom. For builds with user-annotated articulations, posed method allows an agent to create snapshot of the build with joints set to specified articulation parameters, to validate physical feasibility under joint motion. Posing works with models whose kinematic structure forms tree. 3.2. Building with BrickLayer BrickWright is framework for agentic brick build creation using BrickLayer. It provides single agent with set of tools and prompts it to create build by writing and revising single Python file in plan-execute-validate loop, inspired by Articraft [59]. The BrickWright environment exposes the tools validate, which runs agent-written tests alongside fixed collision and floating checks; render, which renders the build into multi-view sheet or from single specified view; and finalize, which marks the build as finished. In its system prompt, BrickWright instructs an agent to make short internal plan, then write Python file, build.py, containing two functions: create build(), which returns LegoBuild, and run tests(), which runs set of agent-written tests against the completed build. After creating build.py, the agent is instructed to iteratively call validate and edit the build file until all tests pass, then call render; if it judges the render satisfactory, it should then call finalize; otherwise, it should revise build.py and repeat validation. Besides these instructions, BrickWright includes only the BrickLayer documentation in its system prompt, and the input text or image in user prompt. It does not provide the agent with detailed planning advice, complete build examples, or building tips beyond the plan-execute-validate loop; the loop alone is sufficient for even lightweight agents to produce feasible build. BrickWright can be used alongside commercial frameworks such as Codex, which allows general file access and script execution. However, to demonstrate its utility alone, we provide the agent with only two additional tools during experiments: read / write / insert / edit build to read and modify build.py, and explore to run Python snippet with BrickLayer and the written LegoBuild in scope, returning its output as text. 4. Experiments We compare BrickWright against two types of baselines: specially trained text-to-brick models (BrickGPT [37] and BrickNet [19]) and pre-trained agentic methods (Articraft [59], OpenAIs Codex, and Anthropics Claude Code). We evaluate the physical feasibility and prompt adherence of the output brick builds. Throughout evaluation, we use the BrickNet-512 [19] dataset, which contains 512 text prompts 5 Figure 4. Qualitative ablation results. Red outlines in insets indicate mesh intersections. See Sec. for input text prompts. created by VLM captioning of human-made brick builds. Technical details. To test agents with range of capabilities, we run experiments with Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna (lightweight), GPT-6.1 Sol (balanced), and GPT-6 Astra (frontier). All agents use High reasoning. Figure examples use Astra unless otherwise specified. Agents are instructed to create builds with no collisions or floaters, and to ensure the build is connected if it comprises one object. Codex and Claude Code baselines may read, write, and execute arbitrary files in workspace directory, which initially contains only the LDraw documentation [21] and the library of LDraw parts [22], including part meshes. BrickWright agents are only allowed to read and modify the output build.py and execute text-output-only Python snippets; they have no access to the LDraw documentation or LDraw part library beyond the searchable parts list exposed by BrickLayer. Agentic methods have budget of $5 per sample; for samples that reach the budget, we use the latest completed build, whether valid or invalid. Only Luna w/o assembly API (2 samples) and Astra with Codex (1 sample), Articraft (34 samples), and full BrickWright (2 samples) reached this limit. As Articraft is intended for primitive-based 3D generation, we minimally modify it to use library of LDraw part meshes rather than mesh primitives. Invalid operations on physical parts (e.g., scaling) are disabled, as are collision checks, which yield false positives for coupled bricks, and watertightness checks, which fail on library meshes. We adjust Articrafts system prompt to reword phrases that do not work with brick builds, such as allowing geometry overlaps. Metrics. We report metrics on physical feasibility as defined in Sec. 3; prompt adherence as judged by VQAScore [28], Perception Encoder [3], and SigLIP 2 [43]; average brick count per build; and average time and cost per prompt. Validity and connectivity are first evaluated using BrickLayers validator. Then, to independently verify the metrics accuracy, we flag potential false positives for review by human experienced with LEGO design. Potential false positives include collisions resolved by tested shift of at most 0.2 mm and disconnected components containing parts without connector annotations. Human review increases collisionfree rates by 0.2 percentage points for BrickNet and Claude Code (Haiku), 1.4 for Codex (Sol), and 1.0 for Codex (Astra). It reduces mean component counts by 0.13 for Codex (Sol), 0.10 for Codex (Astra), and 0.12 for Articraft; changes for the remaining methods are below 0.02 components per build. Numbers in Tab. 1 are post-review. 4.1. Baseline comparison Compared to vanilla agent baselines, builds produced by BrickWright-equipped agents exhibit greatly improved physical feasibility with broadly comparable token costs (Tab. 1). Impressively, the lightweight model Luna, which has only 9% baseline validity rate, achieves 100% validity when used with BrickWright. This increase in physical validity is not accompanied by significant decrease in complexity or fidelity; on average, BrickWright agents use more bricks and more unique parts than vanilla agent baselines, while improving prompt adherence for lightweight models (Haiku, Luna) and maintaining it for powerful models (Sol, Astra). These gains hold even with BrickWrights minimal harness, whereas Codex and Claude Code can read, write, and execute arbitrary files. BrickWright-equipped agents additionally outperform specially trained text-to-brick models in overall feasibility and prompt adherence. The Articraft baseline, which is intended for digital 3D assets, yields comparable prompt adherence but worse physical validity at more than twice the cost of BrickWright. The visual results in Fig. 6 show how BrickWright reduces physical artifacts for all agent backends and improves the coherence of builds created by lightweight agents. On average, most BrickWright agents use 23 validate calls; Luna uses 45 (Tab. 1). 4.2. Ablation study We ablate BrickLayers two key components: the assembly API and the validator. In our first ablation, w/o assembly API, agents write program that creates an LDraw file without using BrickLayers assembly functions. The LegoBuild abstraction is removed from BrickLayer, leaving only part search and physical validation, and its docu6 achieve 100% validity with no assembly API, weaker agents (Luna and Haiku) sometimes give up without finalizing the build, leading to validity scores below 100%. Without an assembly API, Lunas prompt-similarity scores degrade significantly; it often produces simple structures  (Fig. 4)  and its average part count drops from 27.4 to 7.2. Interestingly, merely using BrickLayers API without provided validator boosts validity by up to 44 percentage points from Codex/- Claude Code baselines! The automatic grid-snapping and connector-mating functions provided by BrickLayer help agents, especially lightweight ones, produce valid builds more easily. However, the validator remains crucial component; without it, all agents score below 79% validity (Tab. 1). 4.3. Extensions BrickWright works with image conditions, indoor and outdoor scenes, large-scale builds of more than 29,000 parts, articulated objects, build editing by providing BrickLayer script or LDraw file as input, and special requirements such as being constrained to given set of bricks  (Fig. 5)  . This functionality naturally arises from pre-trained agent capabilities, without needing to update BrickWrights toolkit. 5. Discussion Frontier coding agents are capable of producing aesthetically pleasing LEGO brick builds from text or image prompts. However, even the most capable agents fail to produce physically feasible builds much of the time. Our framework, BrickWright, closes this gap by introducing toolkit for brick build creation and validation. Equipped with BrickWright, even lightweight agents achieve 100% validity on 512 samples tested, while improving prompt adherence at similar cost to agents without BrickWright. We hope this work highlights the importance of well-written construction APIs and physical validation in improving the performance of LLM agents on building tasks. Limitations and future work. Our definition of physical feasibility does not cover valid assembly sequences or stability analysis, which we leave to future work. Though agentic methods outperform specially trained models on brick build generation, they are generally slower and more costly. Effectively distilling the capabilities of powerful agents into smaller, faster models remains an interesting future direction.

sections.content: A. Additional results Table 3 reports valid@k metrics: how often agents reach passing validate call within their first calls, together with mean token usage. With the assembly API, BrickWright agents pass validation in far fewer calls than when writing LDraw directly; for example, 81% of GPT-6.1 Sol builds pass within two calls, compared with 37% without the API. Table 2 breaks down the reasons for failed validate calls. Physical checks account for most failures (6385%), followed by runtime errors (1128%) such as selecting nonexistent connector or specifying an invalid part ID. For GPT agents, most physical failures are due to collisions, while Haikus main failure mode is connectivity. The more capable an agent, the more its physical failure distribution shifts toward collisions, away from floaters and connectivity. Additional qualitative comparisons are given in Fig. 7. B. System prompt and BrickLayer reference Listing 2 shows the system prompt used for BrickWright agents, and Listing 3 shows the user prompt template used for the Codex and Claude Code baselines. The BrickWright prompt also includes the BrickLayer API reference; Listings 4 to 8 show excerpts of the reference documenting the LegoBuild, Element, Placement, LegoGeometry, and Connector classes. Brick build generation with vanilla agents We give short analysis of the brick build creation process of baseline GPT-6 Astra, used with Codex. We inspect the Python programs produced and executed by the agent during generation (whether inline or from file) and classify them as generators and/or validators by using heuristics that trace the programs abstract syntax tree (AST). If program calls write text() or write bytes() on model.ldr file or opens the file in mode with write access, we classify it as generator. If program reads model.ldr and includes an assertion or error involving values derived from model.ldr, we classify it as validator. Out of 512 builds created using prompts from BrickNet-512, 471 (92%) use generator and 424 (83%) use validator. Figure 7. Additional qualitative baseline comparison. See Sec. for text prompts. Red outlines in insets indicate mesh intersections. 3 # BrickWright Instructions You are BrickWright, an expert LEGO builder. Edit build.py so create_build() returns LegoBuild faithful to the request and run_tests() returns its TestContext report. The BrickLayer API reference below describes construction, coordinates, connectors, parts, and colors; use it to resolve API questions. The finished build must meet these requirements: - **No collisions:** parts may touch and mate, but must not interpenetrate. - **No floating parts:** every part must reach the ground through mated connections or supporting surface contacts. Resting on tiles, ledges, and slopes counts; side contact alone does not. Sliding and tipping are not checked. - **Connected:** one connected assembly, unless the request calls for separate pieces. Face contact alone does not connect parts. Use compatible connectors: studs/antistuds, pins/holes, axles, clips/bars, ball joints, and others. Stagger ordinary brick layers or bridge adjacent pieces with shared plate. - **Faithful:** preserve the requested identity, proportions, features, and detail at believable LEGO scale. Do not remove requested features merely to pass checks. ## Checks in build.py The harness independently enforces no floating parts and no collisions on the built model. Connectivity and request-specific checks come from run_tests(). Keep check_no_floating(), check_no_collisions(), and check_connected() in run_tests(). Change expected_components only when the request genuinely calls for multiple assemblies. Add tests.check(name, ok, detail) for measurable requirements; inspect failures and repair the build rather than weakening those requirements. python import bricklayer as bl from brickwright import TestContext def create_build(): build = bl.LegoBuild() build.add(bl.Element("3001", bl.Color.RED)) return build def run_tests(): build = create_build() tests = TestContext(build) tests.check_no_floating() tests.check_no_collisions() tests.check_connected(expected_components=1) # Add checks for this request, e.g. tests.check("over 100 parts", build.brick_count > 100). return tests.report() For articulated builds, declare intended movement with MotionRange on the relevant connections. Optionally add tests.check_motion(samples=5) to sample the annotated ranges for collisions, floating parts, and connector disengagement. Other connections stay rigid, which can produce false positives if they would also move in reality. This check is optional and covers sampled poses, not every intermediate position. build.check_motion() exposes its detailed report for investigation. Static validity checks do not test motion. ## Working method 1. Plan the defining features, rough size, support structure, and specialized parts. 2. Look up catalog parts before using remembered IDs. Use Element(part_id, color) as the normal constructor; size helpers are conveniences. Check their listed argument combinations: dimensions are width-first, and changing orientation requires rotation, not swapping dimensions to an unsupported size. 3. Build in manageable increments. Validate, read each failures detail, and repair it. Use helpers and sub-models for repeated or meaningful assemblies. 4. When rendering is available, inspect the build while working and after the final edit. Physical validity alone does not establish visual fidelity. 5. Run the checks on the finished source. Keep create_build() deterministic and free of file writes so checks, previews, and exports represent the same build. {docs} Listing 2. BrickWright system prompt. {docs} is replaced by tool documentation (e.g. for validate) and the BrickLayer reference. 4 Build LEGO model matching the following description. Save the complete LDraw code in model.ldr in the current workspace. The model must be an assembly of real, existing LEGO parts from the LDraw parts catalogue, referenced by their exact .dat filenames. Use only type-0 comments and metadata and type-1 part or submodel references. Do not emit type-2, type-3, type-4, or type-5 geometry, invent part IDs, or define custom part geometry. If you use MPD submodels, embed them in model.ldr and build each entirely from catalogued parts. Every leaf reference must resolve to real catalogue part. Avoid colliding or floating parts. If the model depicts single object, all its parts must form one connected component through valid LEGO connections. Description: {caption} Listing 3. Codex/Claude Code baseline prompt. {caption} is replaced with the text prompt. #### class LegoBuild(LegoGeometry) LegoBuild(placements: Iterable[Placement] = (), names: Mapping[str, Placement] None = None, steps: Iterable[int] None = None, *, joints: Iterable[Joint] = ()) -> None build or reusable sub-assembly, edited in place. Validity queries update automatically after edits, including edits to nested models. is_valid checks collisions and ground support; is_connected checks whether every part joins through compatible connectors. **Properties** - bounding_box: tuple[Position, Position] -- The physical bounding box spanning every parts, in the models frame. sub-model holding no parts spans nothing, so model with no parts returns (Position.ZERO, Position.ZERO). - brick_count: int -- The total number of bricks in the model. - colliding_placements: tuple[tuple[Placement[Element], Placement[Element]], ...] -- Pairs of placements whose collision volumes overlap. - connected_components: tuple[tuple[Placement[Element], ...], ...] -- The placements grouped by connected component. Each group holds the parts joined to one another through couplings, with the groups and the parts within them in placement order. An empty model has no components. - connectors: frozenset[Connector] -- Unoccupied connector points in this models frame. connector disappears here when it mates with another part, including across nested sub-model boundaries. Covering studs can therefore change the models alignment box and how subsequent parts stack on it. - flattened_joints: tuple[Joint, ...] -- All joint occurrences, with endpoint paths rooted in this model. repeated sub-model contributes distinct records for each occurrence. Use these records as keys to posed when moving nested joint. - flattened_placements: tuple[Placement[Element], ...] -- Every element placement, flattened into this models own frame. Flattening reaches through nested sub-models, so each leaf holds an :class:Element. - floating_placements: tuple[Placement[Element], ...] -- Parts without path to the ground through connectors or contact. The lowest physical extent defines the ground, as in translate_to_ground. The models poses remain unchanged, and returned placements are the original leaves. Mated connectors transmit support in both directions. Surface contacts transmit it from the supporting part to the part resting on it, including on tiles, elevated ledges, and slopes. Sliding and tipping are not checked. - joints: tuple[Joint, ...] -- Connections recorded in this model; nested records stay in their owner. Removing either endpoint, including nested leaf, deletes its record. - names: Mapping[str, Placement] -- The models named placements, keyed by the name each was registered under. live read-only view: names appear as parts are added. - num_connected_components: int -- The number of connected components of the model. - placements: tuple[Placement, ...] -- Every top-level placement in the model, in insertion order. Listing 4. LegoBuild documentation. LegoBuild represents multi-part assembly containing placed elements or sub-builds. It supports adding/removing placements and validating the builds physical feasibility. Excerpt from the BrickLayer API reference included in the BrickWright system prompt. Continued on the next two pages. 5 **Methods** - add(content: Element LegoBuild, position: Position tuple[float, float, float] = Position(0, 0, 0), rotation: Rotation = Rotation.DEG_0, anchor: Anchor = Anchor.FRONT_RIGHT, *, relative_to: NameRef Placement None = None, target_anchor: Anchor = Anchor.FRONT_RIGHT, name: str None = None, index: int None = None) -> Placement -- Place content on the grid; return its placement. position is an absolute (x, y, z) or delta from relative_to (a name, name path, or placement). rotation is the contents own rotation, not relative to the reference. Positions require integer x/y and in whole plates. anchor selects the point on the contents rotated alignment footprint; target_anchor selects the reference point when using relative_to. The default is the front-right minimum corner. An even extents center floors toward that corner: Anchor.CENTER on 4x2 footprint is (1, 0) studs from it. name registers the result; index inserts instead of appending. Content is held by reference. concrete reference is read in this models frame, even if from another model or removed; it is not added automatically. Raises ValueError for off-grid positions, KeyError for missing names, and IndexError for an out-of-range insertion. - add_raw(content: Element LegoBuild, pose: Pose = Pose(rotation=Mat3.IDENTITY, translation=Position(0, 0, 0)), *, name: str None = None, index: int None = None) -> Placement -- Place content at an arbitrary pose without grid checks or re-anchoring. pose maps the contents local frame into this model. An elements origin is its alignment boxs bottom-center; sub-model retains its own frame. Content is shared by reference. name registers the placement and index inserts instead of appending. Invalid insertion indices raise IndexError. - check_motion(*, samples: int = 5, max_samples: int = 10000) -> MotionReport -- Optionally check collisions, floating, and engagement across joint ranges. Samples the Cartesian product, including zero and both limits on every coordinate. Unannotated connections remain rigid, which can flag motions possible with additional flexibility. clear report covers only the samples.
